learn.c1.hint: The key pair (ECDSA P-256) was created in your browser just now. Sign, then edit the text: the signature stops matching.
learn.c1.invalid: Signature no longer matches: the text changed
learn.c1.lib: In SimpleSign every hash and signature uses System.Security.Cryptography, the same cryptography .NET itself uses.
learn.c1.p1: A hash (here SHA-256) turns any content into a short fingerprint. Change one letter and the fingerprint changes completely.
learn.c1.p2: A digital signature is that fingerprint sealed with a private key that only the signer has. Anyone can check the seal with the matching public key, which travels inside the certificate.
learn.c1.title: A fingerprint, then a seal
learn.c2.e.byterange: /ByteRange lists the two signed pieces: from byte 0 for a bytes, and from byte b for c bytes. The gap between them is /Contents.
learn.c2.e.contents: /Contents is a hole reserved for the signature. It is the only part not hashed, because it holds the result of hashing everything else.
learn.c2.e.default: Click a part of the diagram to see what it does.
learn.c2.e.original: Everything before the signature value is hashed: the original pages and the new signature dictionary (signer name, reason, date).
learn.c2.e.tail: After the hole come the rest of the dictionary, the cross-reference table and the trailer. They are hashed too.
learn.c2.p1: A signed PDF is the original file plus an incremental update appended to the end. The update adds a signature field whose value has two key parts.
learn.c2.p2: Because the signed bytes are fixed, any later change to them breaks the signature. New signatures and LTV data are added as further updates, after the signed range.
learn.c2.title: How a PDF carries a signature
learn.c3.e.attrs: What is actually signed: the document hash (messageDigest) and a hash of the signer certificate (signingCertificateV2), so the certificate cannot be swapped.
learn.c3.e.certs: The signer certificate (with the public key and identity, such as the CPF) and usually its issuing chain.
learn.c3.e.chain: The validator takes the public key from the certificate and checks the signature value against the signed attributes.
learn.c3.e.default: Click a box to see what it proves.
learn.c3.e.sig: The private key's output over the DER-encoded signed attributes. RSA, RSA-PSS or ECDSA.
learn.c3.e.unsigned: Added after signing, without breaking it: a timestamp token (RFC 3161) over the signature value proves it existed at that time.
learn.c3.p1: The /Contents holds a CMS SignedData (the same format as a .p7s file). PAdES and CAdES add rules on top of it.
learn.c3.p2: The signature covers the attributes, and the attributes cover the document through messageDigest. That is why a tampered PDF fails the integrity check even though the signature value itself still verifies. You can see this with the inspector and the “tampered” sample.
learn.c3.title: Inside the signature: CMS
learn.c4.e.bb: B-B (basic): the signature and the signer certificate. The signing time is only what the signer claims.
learn.c4.e.blt: B-LT: the validation data (chain, OCSP responses, CRLs) is stored in the PDF's DSS, so it validates even after the CA is offline.
learn.c4.e.blta: B-LTA: a document timestamp seals everything, and can be renewed before its algorithms grow weak. Best for archives.
learn.c4.e.bt: B-T: a Time-Stamping Authority adds a trusted timestamp, proving the signature existed before the certificate expired.
learn.c4.p1: Certificates expire and keys get old. The PAdES baseline levels (ETSI EN 319 142) add evidence so a signature can still be checked years later.
learn.c4.title: Time and the long term: B-B to B-LTA
learn.c5.p1: A valid seal only proves that some key signed. To know who, the validator follows the certificate chain up to a root it trusts, such as the AC Raiz ICP-Brasil, and asks OCSP or CRL whether a certificate was revoked.
learn.c5.p2: The result is one of three indications. Pick a situation:
learn.c5.s.ok: Intact file, trusted chain, not revoked
learn.c5.s.revoked: Certificate revoked before the signing time
learn.c5.s.tampered: The PDF was changed after signing
learn.c5.title: Trust: who vouches for the signer
learn.c5.x.offline: Indeterminate: revocation status could not be checked. Try again later, or sign at B-LT so the evidence is inside the PDF.
learn.c5.x.ok: Every check passed: the document is intact, the signature verifies and the chain reaches a trusted root.
learn.c5.x.revoked: Invalid: the certificate was revoked before the (timestamped) signing time, so the signature cannot be trusted.
learn.c5.x.tampered: Invalid: the hash of the signed bytes no longer matches messageDigest. The file is not the one that was signed.
learn.c5.x.unknown: Indeterminate: the signature is mathematically correct, but nobody trusted vouches for the key. Add the root you trust, or use ICP-Brasil roots.
learn.c6.a3.text: The key cannot be copied out of the device. SimpleSign talks to its PKCS#11 driver; the device signs the hash.
learn.c6.cloud.text: The key lives in the provider's HSM (BirdID, VIDaaS…). The holder approves in the app or browser; only the hash is sent.
learn.c6.deferred.text: Your server prepares the PDF, the user's device signs, and the server finishes. The key never reaches the server.
learn.c6.p1: The signature is the same in every case; what changes is where the private key is and who touches it.
learn.c6.pfx.text: The key is in a password-protected file. Easy for servers and automation; protect the file and the password.
learn.c6.title: Where the private key lives
